analysis.one_liner: Bans new offshore oil and gas drilling off Florida's Gulf and Atlantic coasts.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2008 and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, where it died without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to permanently bar the Interior Department from offering any new oil and gas leases or preleases in the Eastern Gulf of Mexico, the southern South Atlantic Planning Area, and the Straits of Florida Planning Area — the waters off Florida's coasts. It would not have affected leases already issued. The bill was referred to committee the day it was introduced and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the bill would have protected Florida's beaches, fisheries, and coastal tourism economy from the risk of new offshore drilling and the spills, rigs, and industrial activity that come with it. It also would have protected coastal communities and seafood industries that depend on clean water along the state's Gulf and Atlantic coasts.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the Secretary of the Interior from offering oil and gas leasing, preleasing, or any related activity in specified areas of the Eastern Gulf of Mexico, the southern South Atlantic Planning Area, and the Straits of Florida Planning Area.
It writes the ban into the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act itself, making it a permanent statutory prohibition rather than a policy that an administration could change.
The bill preserves rights under any oil and gas leases issued before enactment, so it targets only new drilling activity.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the cost would have fallen on oil and gas companies, which would have been denied access to potentially large offshore reserves near Florida, and indirectly on consumers and the federal treasury, which forgoes leasing revenue. Some argued the country would have less domestic energy supply at a time of high prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have removed potentially large domestic oil and gas reserves from development, which supporters of drilling argued was especially costly amid the 2008 energy price spike.
It restricted federal leasing across three large offshore planning areas, affecting energy production well beyond Florida's immediate coastal waters.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded a permanent ban on new drilling near Florida's coasts against forgone oil and gas production in those areas. For people who live, work, and vacation on Florida's coasts, the protection against spills and industrialization was the central benefit; for the energy industry and those prioritizing domestic supply, the reserves were the loss. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how one weighs environmental and tourism risk against energy supply, and the bill itself never received a hearing or debate to test it.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: the House Natural Resources Committee referred it to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee two days after introduction, and nothing further happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Kathy Castor introduced the Florida Coastal Protection Act on April 22, 2008.
The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources the same day.
On April 24, 2008, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress with no further action.
No other member cosponsored the bill, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests were better off: with no drilling ban enacted, the areas off Florida's coast remained available for potential future leasing, and no restrictions were added to federal offshore leasing law.

for.name: Rep. Kathy Castor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 22, 2008 to bar new offshore oil and gas leasing off Florida's coasts.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it was sent to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee and never received a hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had no cosponsors and no recorded votes, so no party-level support or opposition is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have permanently barred new leasing in the Eastern Gulf of Mexico, the southern South Atlantic, and the Straits of Florida, locking the industry out of those offshore reserves. Its defeat left those areas open to potential future leasing.

industries.industry: Florida coastal tourism and commercial fishing
industries.note: The bill would have protected the beaches, fisheries, and clean coastal waters that Florida's tourism and seafood economies depend on from new drilling and spill risk. Its failure left that protection to exist only as a temporary administrative moratorium rather than law.
